questions.itemBody:
Political units in the history of West Africa

Note: this is an extract from a General Training Reading text on the subject of political units in the history of West Africa

Some of Africa’s earliest substantial masonry structures outside Egypt were built in West Africa. The fact that they were constructed demonstrates the existence of a sedentary and complex political unit. At Dhar Tichitt and Dhar Oualata, in modern Mauritania, a new chiefdom developed (around 2000–800 BC) in a deteriorating environment where arable land and pasturage for animals were at a premium. A four-tier settlement hierarchy has been discovered (that is, towns and other settlements at four levels of importance, based on size, function, and type of building), with the largest regional centers exceeding 220 acres (90 ha) in area. The evolution of Tichitt-Oualata society remains unclear, obscured by the poor condition of settlement sites. Competing hypotheses include long-term development in the area, rapid evolution, or immigration from elsewhere. Evidence points to the importance of mixed farming – both crops and animals. Inorganic wealth lay in beads, bracelets and small stone axes. Unfortunately, none of the region’s many tumuli* have yet been excavated. It would appear that the collapse of Tichitt-Oualata around 800 BC was brought about both by the increasing drying of the earth in the region and growing harassment from interlopers from outside.

During the first millennium BC, the advent of metallurgy added further impetus to the growth of complex societies south of the Sahara Desert. Indeed, precious metals were to play a key role in international trade between West Africa and the Mediterranean world, and between East Africa and Asia, throughout the late first and early second millennia AD. At a regional level, iron and copper were crucial materials for making both practical and prestige objects. Coupled with trade in ivory, the control of metallurgical commodities supplanted subsistence farming as the power basis of African elites from the beginning of the first millennium AD.

The empire of Ghana existed before Arab geographers began to write of West Africa in the eighth century AD. Its origins and extent remain unclear. The ruins of one of its capitals, Kumbi-Saleh, lie in southeastern Mauritania; yet the most substantive settlement clusters known from the first millennium AD rest within the bounds of the Middle Niger river in neighboring Mali. Earlier scholarly thought placed Ghana as a state founded by Arab traders from North Africa, but recent research has emphasized the indigenous development of regional trade webs long before the Arab conquest of North Africa around AD 750.

Undoubtedly, the Middle Niger’s best-excavated site is that of Jenné-Jeno (250 BC to AD 1400). Here, trade with adjoining regions in commodities such as copper, iron, and sandstone is in evidence by AD 500. Additionally, by AD 800, local craft specialization and a regional hierarchy centered on Jenné-Jeno point to an urban status for the site. However, Jenné-Jeno is only one of many impressive settlements now known from the Middle Niger. The occupation of such sites continued through the time of Ghana's Islamic successor states, the empire of Mali (AD 1250–1600) and the empire of Songhai (AD 1375–1600). Future work is likely to confirm the view that the heart of the empire of Ghana, like that of the Malinke empire of Mali, lay not in its trade centers in the Sahara but closer to the resource centers of the Middle Niger.

While Jenné-Jeno was flourishing, spectacular developments were also taking place in the West African forest. Although limited excavations have only begun to hint at the political organization of Nigerian societies during the late first millennium AD, their richness and artistic expertise have been well demonstrated at the site of Igbo-Ukwu. Here an elaborate burial and a storehouse of regalia have been excavated, both holding superb brass castings and thousands of glass beads. The presence of such wealth hints at a well-organized system of trade, remarkably accomplished craft specialists, and a wealthy elite, but we know little of settlements in the region until the emergence of the state of Ife around AD 1100.

*tumuli: small burial mounds made of stone and earth
